messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kwame is a 55-year-old Ghanaian-American painter, married for nearly three decades, who presented for psychological assessment approximately eight months after the sudden death of his adult son, Kofi, who collapsed without warning from a cardiac event at the age of thirty-one. Kofi had come to the worksite one afternoon to bring his father lunch — a small habit they had kept for years — and Kwame was on a scaffold when he heard shouting below. By the time he climbed down, Kofi was on the ground. Kwame knelt beside him, held his face, and watched the paramedics arrive and work with increasing urgency before the effort finally stopped. The last image burned into him was not the moment of collapse but the stillness afterward — the particular quality of light on the concrete, the yellow of the ambulance doors standing open, and the sound of the radio crackling in the silence that followed. His PCL-5 score of 67 reflects a presentation of considerable severity.

In the months that followed, Kwame continued working because he did not know what else to do with himself. Painting had always been physical, meditative, something he could lose himself in — but the worksite had become a landscape of ambush. The smell of the afternoon, the particular angle of sunlight on a concrete floor, the sound of a vehicle pulling up — any of these could stop him mid-stroke. When an ambulance passed the building where he was working, the sound of the siren did not simply startle him; it pulled the scene back with full force, the visual memories arriving as images rather than narrative — Kofi's face, the open doors, the yellow — accompanied by a wave of grief so overwhelming that Kwame had to descend from the scaffold and stand in a corner until it passed. And each time a trigger struck — the siren, the light, the smell of a warm afternoon — the thought arrived with it, unbidden and absolute: this is what your life is now, and this is all it will ever be. The sensory cues did not merely summon the memory; they seemed to ratify the belief that something irreversible had happened to him, that the man who had climbed scaffolds and shared lunches with his son was simply gone. His colleagues noticed. He had begun taking longer breaks, positioning himself away from the street-facing side of buildings, and on two occasions had left a job early without explanation. A contract was not renewed.

These intrusions did not stay at work. At home in the evenings, Kwame found himself unable to settle. He felt on guard inside his own house in a way he could not fully explain to his wife, Adwoa — a persistent bodily readiness, muscles held taut, as though danger were not past but imminent. Living at that pitch of alertness, he found that the world had grown dense with cues he could not stop reading as warnings — a car door slamming in the street outside, a neighbour's voice raised briefly in laughter, the particular quality of afternoon light falling through the kitchen window. The background hum of threat he carried everywhere meant that stimuli which would once have passed through him without purchase now snagged, each one briefly indistinguishable from the signals that had accompanied the worst afternoon of his life. Nights were the worst. The darkness seemed to strip away whatever thin reassurance the daylight provided, and he lay awake with his body braced, the images returning unbidden. When the grief came at night without any clear image attached — just the weight of it, arriving in the chest like something physical — he found it almost harder to bear than the pictures, because there was nothing to locate or push away. The heightened vigilance itself seemed to drag the memories closer, as though his nervous system, already scanning for threat, kept finding it in the archive of that afternoon. But the memories, once surfaced, did not release him cleanly — they left residue. After an image had broken through, even the most neutral features of the worksite felt freighted: the angle of a shadow, the sound of a tool dropped on concrete, the particular quality of silence between sounds. The memory seemed to seed the environment with new triggers, so that the hours following an intrusion were the hours in which he was most likely to be ambushed again.

What frightened Kwame most, in the way that a man frightened of his own mind is frightened, was what the memories and the grief seemed to confirm about his life. He had come to believe, with a quiet and terrible certainty, that his life had been destroyed — not damaged or interrupted, but ended in some essential way on that afternoon. Once that conviction had settled into him, the world outside seemed to reorganise itself around it — almost anything could become a signal confirming what he already knew. The yellow of a construction vehicle, the particular stillness of a midday break, the sound of a radio crackling from a nearby cab: things he would once have registered and dismissed now snagged and held him, because his belief that everything had already been lost made every ordinary cue feel like a reminder he was not permitted to ignore. He felt like a stranger to himself, unable to recognise the man who had climbed scaffolds with confidence and eaten lunch with his son. This conviction of ruin fed back into the vigilance: if his life was already over, then every ordinary threat felt more credible, every night more dangerous. And the appraisals made the memories more unbearable when they came — each image seemed to serve as evidence for what he already believed. When a neighbour mentioned losing a family member in passing conversation, Kwame felt the isolation close around him like a wall. He had stopped attending church, where such talk was common, and had grown quieter at home in ways Adwoa could not reach.

It was Adwoa who finally persuaded him to seek help, after he woke shouting on a night she described as the worst she had witnessed. Kwame came to the intake session composed but exhausted. He did not ask to feel happy. What he said, quietly, near the end of the first session, was that he wanted to know whether it was still possible to be someone — whether anything of the man he had been before that afternoon on the worksite could be recovered, or whether he had already lost that too.
